svg.text: Software (long-lived; testable off the target)
OSAL
OS abstraction layer
HAL
hardware abstraction layer
Operating system / RTOS
(a detail)
Firmware
(PAL inside; a detail)
Hardware (evolves; parts obsolete, cheaper, faster)
Firmware versus software
Doug Schmidt: 'Although software does not wear out, firmware and hardware
become obsolete'; Grenning adds that software can be destroyed from within
by unmanaged dependencies on firmware and hardware. Code is firmware
because of what it depends on and how hard it is to change, not because it
sits in ROM; non-embedded developers write firmware too (SQL buried in
code, spread platform dependencies, Android apps mixing business logic with
the Android API)
The App-titude test
Kent Beck: first make it work, then make it right, then make it fast; Fred Brooks:
plan to throw one away; getting an app to work is the 'App-titude test': a flat
file of mixed ISRs, domain logic, flash storage and sensor code, testable only on
the target, passes it without a clean architecture
Target-hardware bottleneck
hardware may be developed alongside the software, may be absent or buggy, and if
code can only be tested on the target progress slows; a clean embedded architecture
is a testable embedded architecture, with HAL and OSAL as seams for off-target
tests
HAL: its API is shaped by the software's needs (name and value pairs, not flash bytes; Indicate_LowBattery() rather than Led_TurnOn(5)); layers contain layers (a
repeating fractal); never reveal hardware details to its user. Processor: vendor C extensions (IE, SBUF0, TI_0) are not C; confine them to firmware, use stdint.h, and a
processor abstraction layer (PAL). OS: an OSAL protects against RTOS changes and offers a common structure (message passing instead of handcrafted concurrency). Use
headers as interfaces, keep implementation details out of them, and replace thousands of #ifdef BOARD_V2 repetitions (a DRY violation) with HAL interfaces bound by the
linker or at runtime.
